Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma

vignette: The afternoon Javier’s life fractured began with the relentless staccato of automatic fire across a shattered field hospital. He had been navigating smoke-choked corridors, shoving stretchers toward the rear exit as concrete dust choked the air. When the fire intensified, medics and civilians pressed against him, a suffocating wall of panicked bodies in the collapsing stairwell. Later, a convoy secured the perimeter, and a nurse handed him a canteen with a smile of exhausted relief. Javier remembered his chest tightening instead of relaxing; the sudden shift from danger to brief safety felt fundamentally wrong, as if the calm were a lure. When mortar fire followed minutes later, he realized that the chaotic noise, the crushing physical proximity, and that jarring flash of relief were the exact frequencies of his collapse. Months later, Javier returned to Florida to run his family’s import logistics firm, but safety never held. When a delivery truck backfired on the interstate, his body locked, and the memory of the stairwell instantly flooded him. The moment the auditory intrusions and crushing physical proximity of client meetings became unbearable, Javier instinctively reached for his coping mechanisms. He began walking into the loading bay each morning with a heavy revolver clipped to his belt, the cold metal against his hip the only thing that made sudden, sharp sounds bearable. When the distress peaked, his mind automatically turned inward. He paced his office after hours, circling relentlessly around why he survived while others did not, his thoughts trapped in a loop of meaning-making until exhaustion forced sleep. These strategies soon became the architecture of his dread. Javier’s habit of manufacturing arguments with his warehouse foremen served as a deliberate distraction. By picking fights over shipping delays, he forced his nervous system into high alert, temporarily drowning out the intrusive threat sounds and claustrophobic pressure. Yet this tactical avoidance kept his threat detection system permanently primed. Because he was always bracing for conflict or dissecting his survival, the environment sharpened into a hazard map. The hum of forklifts in his own distribution center now registered as imminent gunfire, and the routine proximity of his sales team walking past his glass office walls triggered the same suffocating dread as the collapsed stairwell. By the time his wife noticed him flinching at celebratory company dinners, Javier’s business was fracturing under his vigilance. When a client shared a joke and the table erupted in laughter, Javier’s jaw clenched; that sudden burst of shared positive emotion made him feel unmoored, as if his internal alarm were misfiring against the room’s joy. He stopped attending staff gatherings because that dissonance left him unable to breathe in crowded rooms. His attempts to control his environment through armed security and preemptive confrontations had isolated him from partners and eroded his marriage, leaving him in a solitary, hyper-awake state. He finally booked an appointment not because the intrusions stopped, but because he could no longer separate past from present. Sitting in the waiting room, his hand resting on the concealed holster beneath his jacket, he hoped for relief, though he feared that lowering his guard would strip away the only armor he knew how to wield.
